data.targetWord: Suffering or harm caused by human choices and actions, such as war, theft, cruelty, or injustice

examples.en-GB: Bullying and warfare are examples of moral evil — they result from human decisions.

data.targetWord: Suffering caused by natural processes rather than human choices, such as earthquakes, floods, or disease

examples.en-GB: An earthquake that destroys a city is natural evil — no human chose to cause it.

data.targetWord: The human capacity to make real moral choices — to choose good or evil — rather than following pre-programmed responses

examples.en-GB: The free will defence argues that God allows evil because genuine goodness requires freedom to choose otherwise.

data.targetWord: The inner sense of right and wrong; the moral voice that guides a person's choices and responses

examples.en-GB: A person's conscience may prevent them from lying even when they could get away with it.

topics: Good and Evil: Problem of Suffering

data.targetWord: A philosophical challenge: if God is all-powerful and all-loving, why does evil and suffering exist in the world?

examples.en-GB: The problem of evil is a key challenge for religious believers who hold God to be both all-powerful and all-loving.

topics: Good and Evil: Problem of Suffering

data.targetWord: An attempt to justify belief in a good God despite the existence of evil and suffering in the world

examples.en-GB: The soul-making theodicy argues that suffering enables moral and spiritual growth.

topics: Good and Evil: Problem of Suffering

data.targetWord: The argument that God allows suffering because the world is a 'vale of soul-making' where humans develop morally and spiritually through challenges

examples.en-GB: The soul-making theodicy, associated with Irenaeus and Hick, argues that suffering has a purpose in human development.

topics: Good and Evil: Justice and Forgiveness

data.targetWord: Fairness; ensuring people receive what they deserve; protecting the vulnerable and holding wrongdoers accountable

examples.en-GB: Justice requires that harm is named and that appropriate consequences follow.

topics: Good and Evil: Justice and Forgiveness

data.targetWord: Choosing to release resentment and let go of the desire for revenge, without necessarily excusing the wrongdoing

examples.en-GB: Forgiveness does not mean pretending harm did not happen — it is about the victim's freedom from bitterness.

topics: Good and Evil: Justice and Forgiveness

data.targetWord: Restoring a broken relationship and rebuilding trust after harm has been done

examples.en-GB: Reconciliation requires genuine apology, changed behaviour, and time — it is not the same as forgiveness.

topics: Good and Evil: Justice and Forgiveness

data.targetWord: A penalty imposed on someone who has done wrong, which may serve as retribution, deterrence, or rehabilitation

examples.en-GB: Punishment is one tool of justice, but justice also requires fairness, not just severity.

topics: Good and Evil: Justice and Forgiveness

data.targetWord: Showing compassion and leniency rather than giving the full punishment deserved

examples.en-GB: A judge who gives a reduced sentence because of difficult circumstances is showing mercy.

topics: Good and Evil: Justice and Forgiveness

data.targetWord: A process where the offender faces the person they harmed and works to repair the damage, focusing on repair rather than purely punishment

examples.en-GB: Restorative justice brings offenders and victims together to discuss harm and find a path to repair.

data.targetWord: Being accountable for one's actions and their consequences; accepting that one's choices matter

examples.en-GB: Taking responsibility means admitting harm done and working to make it right.

data.targetWord: Caring deeply about the suffering of others and being moved to help them

examples.en-GB: Compassion is a core virtue in Buddhism, Christianity, and most ethical traditions.

data.targetWord: Pain, loss, or distress — physical, emotional, or spiritual — that is a central concern in religious and ethical thought

examples.en-GB: Different religions give different explanations for why suffering exists and how to respond to it.

data.targetWord: The Islamic virtue of patient endurance and steadfast acceptance of God's will during times of hardship and suffering

examples.en-GB: The Qur'an promises rewards to those who practise sabr in the face of hardship.

data.targetWord: The parable of Jesus in Luke 15, in which a father forgives and welcomes back his wasteful son — used to illustrate God's unconditional forgiveness

examples.en-GB: The Prodigal Son parable is often used to explain that Christian forgiveness is unconditional and not dependent on merit.

data.targetWord: A decision about right and wrong in which a person has the genuine freedom to choose differently

examples.en-GB: Deciding whether to tell the truth when lying would benefit you is a moral choice.

data.targetWord: The Buddhist concept of suffering and dissatisfaction; the first Noble Truth, teaching that all existence involves unsatisfactoriness

examples.en-GB: The Buddhist response to suffering begins by acknowledging dukkha as a universal feature of life.

items: If God is all-powerful, God could prevent all evil and suffering
If God is all-loving, God would want to prevent all evil and suffering
Evil and suffering clearly exist in the world
Therefore, either God is not all-powerful, not all-loving, or does not exist

items: Harm is done and the wrongdoer is identified
The offender and victim meet in a structured setting
The offender hears the real impact of their actions
Apology and a plan for repair are agreed

data.title: Arrange these stages of an ethical response to wrongdoing in a logical order
items: Harm is done — by human choice or natural cause
The harm is named and those responsible are identified
Justice is applied — consequences are decided
Forgiveness and reconciliation are considered where possible
